evidence_quotes.quote: Based on literature, this report aims to fill the knowledge gap pertaining to both water resources (as addressed in water law) and infrastructure development (key to access sufficient water when and where needed) by developing a grounded understanding of customary water tenure, with the rural farming or pastoralist community as the unit of analysis.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 12 of 45 (Relevance to Statutory Water Law and Other Legislation)
evidence_quotes.quote: The micro-scale de minimis water uses for domestic purposes and basic productive uses are exempt from the obligation to apply for a permit. However, this implies a weak legal status or the total invisibility of those users, who include the most vulnerable (van Koppen and Schreiner 2018).

Moreover, since mainly literature in English was studied, evidence from Francophone and Arabic cases was limited. There is no claim that the over 100 cases cited are in any way exhaustive. Substantive further literature review and field research is required.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 27 of 45 (Customary Water Infrastructure Development - Membership)
evidence_quotes.quote: Members have user rights to the water and can co-decide on water distribution rules and their implementation, provided they comply with obligations to contribute cash, labor or otherwise to the construction.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 32 of 45 (Cross-sectoral Collaboration to Accelerate Water Services for Multiple Uses on Homesteads)
evidence_quotes.quote: In customary water tenure, households use water to meet both domestic and productive needs. Even below basic service levels, livestock and the use and reuse of water for cultivation may have a higher priority than regular home bathing.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural community and household water service access for drinking, domestic, and multiple productive uses (including supported self supply, wells, boreholes, and communal gravity piped systems) across sub-Saharan Africa.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain wording, it examines legal, institutional, and governance arrangements for rural water management (customary water tenure and statutory water law). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it specifically examines rule-type mechanisms directly governing water access, including statutory water permitting/licensing rules and de minimis exemptions, customary socio-territorial water tenure, rights of way to water sources, hydraulic property rights, membership/joining fee conditions, and rotation/exclusion rules in communal self-supply infrastructure. (Both decision and plain_criterion2_decision are 'exclude' solely because Criterion 3 fails under E05.)
criterion_notes.c3: No primary empirical data and not a systematic empirical synthesis (exclude E05). The report is a conceptual and policy overview based on an unsystematic narrative review of secondary literature (over 100 illustrative published cases) with no primary fieldwork/dataset and no systematic search strategy, eligibility criteria, screening protocol, or structured synthesis methodology.
criterion_notes.c4: Does not report primary empirical outcomes or systematically synthesized outcome estimates; although it narratively cites secondary literature illustrating household/community water access, rotation, rationing, and disconnection of non-payers, no empirical outcome measurement is conducted or systematically synthesized.
criterion_notes.c5: As a conceptual/narrative literature review and policy report rather than a primary empirical study or systematic review, there is no identifiable primary study sample or systematic synthesis design linking a defined empirical sample's exposure and outcome.

study_design: Narrative literature review and conceptual policy/legal report (non-empirical, non-systematic)
country: Sub-Saharan Africa (multi-country narrative overview citing secondary literature from South Africa, Tanzania, Kenya, Ethiopia, Zambia, Malawi, Zimbabwe, Uganda, Ghana, Burkina Faso, Mozambique, Eritrea, Niger, and Nigeria)
population_and_sample: not reported (conceptual unit of analysis is rural farming and pastoralist communities in sub-Saharan Africa; no primary empirical sample or systematic review study sample)
exposure: Customary water tenure rules (socio-territorial claims, rights of way, hydraulic property rights, communal infrastructure membership and rotation rules) and statutory water permit systems (discussed conceptually via secondary literature)
outcome: not reported (narrative citations to secondary studies on household/community water access, sharing, and self supply, with no primary or systematically synthesized empirical outcome data)
rationale: This IWMI Research Report matches the record metadata and is accessible in full text. It examines rural community and household water access (including domestic water and homestead self supply) and rule-type legal/institutional mechanisms governing access (customary water tenure, rights of way, hydraulic property/membership rules, and statutory water permit systems vs. de minimis exemptions), satisfying Criteria 1 and 2 under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. However, it fails Criterion 3 (E05: No empirical evidence): the report presents a conceptual framework and policy/legal reform argument illustrated by an unsystematic narrative review of secondary literature ('There is no claim that the over 100 cases cited are in any way exhaustive. Substantive further literature review and field research is required'), with no primary data collection and no systematic empirical synthesis methods.
